# Macromolecular Tissue Volume and the g-ratio

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

---

This chapter develops two related quantitative measures of white-matter tissue.
Macromolecular tissue volume (MTV) estimates the fraction of a voxel that is
*not* water — the space taken up by myelin, membranes, and other macromolecules.
The g-ratio combines a myelin estimate with an axon estimate to report a
geometric property of the fiber that governs conduction speed. Both build on the
quantitative T1 and proton-density mapping introduced earlier, and both require
careful removal of the coil-related intensity bias that contaminates raw MR
images.

## Macromolecular tissue volume

The motivation for MTV is microstructural. A very small part of a white-matter
voxel contains axons wrapped in many layers of myelin, and each myelin membrane
is a lipid bilayer surrounded by water (@fig-ch66-mtv-myelin-water). The more
myelin and other macromolecular material a voxel contains, the less room is left
for water. If we can measure the water fraction accurately, then one minus that
fraction — the macromolecular tissue volume — is a measure of tissue content.

![A white-matter voxel is dominated by myelinated axons. Each myelin membrane is
a lipid bilayer (~5 nm) surrounded by water (~1 nm layers); more myelin means
less space for water.](images/ch66/mtv-myelin-water.png){#fig-ch66-mtv-myelin-water}

The water fraction is estimated from proton density (PD), and here the practical
difficulty appears. Raw scanner images are not quantitative: their brightness
falls off systematically from the center to the edge because of the receive
coil's spatially varying sensitivity (@fig-ch66-mtv-raw-image-bias). Recovering a
true PD map means separating this coil gain from the tissue signal, not merely
cosmetically flattening the image.

![A raw T1-weighted image. Brightness varies from edge to center because of the
receive coil's spatially varying sensitivity — an artifact that must be removed
quantitatively to estimate proton density.](images/ch66/mtv-raw-image-bias.png){#fig-ch66-mtv-raw-image-bias}

The starting point is quantitative T1 mapping. A single T1-weighted image
confounds the tissue's T1 with the scan parameters and coil gain; acquiring
several images at different flip angles and fitting the spoiled gradient-echo
signal equation separates these factors, yielding clean T1 and PD (M0) maps
(@fig-ch66-qmri-measuring-t1). The image intensity can be written schematically as
a function of coil gain, scan parameters, and tissue properties, and the fit
disentangles them.

![Quantitative T1. The same brain at several flip angles shows that intensity
depends on scan parameters as well as tissue T1. Fitting the signal equation
across flip angles separates coil gain, T1, and proton
density.](images/ch66/qmri-measuring-t1.png){#fig-ch66-qmri-measuring-t1}

Estimating PD from the data is an ill-posed problem, and it is instructive to see
why. In simulation without noise the coil sensitivity and PD can be recovered
perfectly; add realistic noise and the estimates degrade badly, because a
flexible model fits the noise rather than the signal, and the cross-validation
accuracy collapses (@fig-ch66-pd-overfitting-regularization). The remedy is
regularization: adding a constraint from something else we know to be true. Here
the useful prior is the physical relationship between T1 and PD, which lets a
biophysically regularized fit recover accurate PD maps.

![Overfitting in PD estimation. Without noise the fit is perfect (top); with
noise, an unconstrained fit tracks the noise and fails (bottom). A regularization
constraint is needed.](images/ch66/pd-overfitting-regularization.png){#fig-ch66-pd-overfitting-regularization}

Is the resulting MTV a genuine measure of tissue volume, independent of the
particular chemistry? A calibration experiment says largely yes. Working with the
chemistry department to build lipid phantoms — with and without inserted
cholesterol — the measured lipid volume tracks the calculated lipid volume along
the line of identity regardless of whether cholesterol is present
(@fig-ch66-mtv-lipid-calibration). MTV measures how much space the macromolecules
occupy, not what they are made of.

![Lipid-phantom calibration. Measured lipid volume matches calculated lipid
volume along the identity line whether or not cholesterol is added, showing that
MTV is largely insensitive to lipid chemistry.](images/ch66/mtv-lipid-calibration.png){#fig-ch66-mtv-lipid-calibration}

Chemistry does leave a separate signature, however, in how strongly the water
interacts with the macromolecular surfaces. The same tissue volume can produce a
different surface-interaction rate. Defining the volume of interacting protons as
$VIP = (T1_m - T1_f)/(T1_c - T1_f)$ — where $T1_m$ is the measured T1, $T1_f$ the
T1 of free water, and $T1_c$ a calibration value — and the surface interaction
rate as $SIR = VIP/MTV$, cholesterol-containing samples show a higher interaction
rate at the same lipid volume (@fig-ch66-mtv-vip-sir). MTV and SIR are
complementary: one reports how much material is present, the other reports
something about its surface chemistry.

![Same volume, different signature. VIP/SIR increases with cholesterol at matched
lipid volume, so the surface-interaction rate carries chemical information beyond
the volume itself.](images/ch66/mtv-vip-sir.png){#fig-ch66-mtv-vip-sir}

### Why not just use diffusion?

The usual way to characterize white matter is diffusion imaging, but FA is not a
clean measure of tissue content. FA varies enormously along a single tract, and
the largest swings come from *geometry* — crossing fibers — rather than from
myelin. Where callosal fibers cross the corticospinal tract, FA drops sharply,
and the rank ordering of subjects changes from place to place along the tract
(@fig-ch66-diffusion-fa-along-tract). MTV is attractive precisely because it
responds to tissue content more directly than FA does.

![FA varies strongly along the corticospinal tract, dropping where callosal fibers
cross it. The largest FA changes reflect fiber geometry, not tissue
content.](images/ch66/diffusion-fa-along-tract.png){#fig-ch66-diffusion-fa-along-tract}

Combining a tract model with quantitative maps gives tract profiles that can be
compared against a normative range. In multiple sclerosis patients, the
macromolecular tissue volume fraction (MTVF) along the corticospinal tract falls
below the control distribution at specific locations, and the diffusion and FA
profiles add complementary information about disease stage
(@fig-ch66-mtv-tract-profile-ms).

![Tract profiles in two MS patients (red) against the control distribution
(gray). MTVF, a diffusion index, and FA each drop below the normal range at
particular tract locations.](images/ch66/mtv-tract-profile-ms.png){#fig-ch66-mtv-tract-profile-ms}

## The g-ratio

Myelin does two things for an axon: it speeds conduction and it lowers the energy
cost of signaling. Conduction velocity rises with fiber caliber, but only for
myelinated axons — the unmyelinated curve stays low across the whole range of
diameters (@fig-ch66-gratio-conduction-speed). The precise speed depends on how
much myelin wraps a given axon.

![Conduction speed versus fiber caliber. Myelinated fibers (upper curve) conduct
far faster than unmyelinated fibers (lower curve), and the relationship depends on
myelin amount.](images/ch66/gratio-conduction-speed.png){#fig-ch66-gratio-conduction-speed}

The amount of myelin is not arbitrary: across axons there is a consistent
relationship between myelin thickness and axon perimeter, so larger axons carry
proportionally thicker sheaths (@fig-ch66-gratio-axon-myelin-relation). This
regularity is captured by a single number, the g-ratio.

![Myelin thickness scales with axon perimeter across a population of fibers
(Fraher, 1972), motivating a single geometric summary — the
g-ratio.](images/ch66/gratio-axon-myelin-relation.png){#fig-ch66-gratio-axon-myelin-relation}

The **g-ratio** is the ratio of the inner (axon) to the outer (axon + myelin)
diameter of a myelinated fiber (@fig-ch66-gratio-geometry). It matters because it
sets the balance between conduction speed and the metabolic and spatial cost of
myelin. It can be estimated from MRI by combining a myelin volume fraction (MVF)
and an axon volume fraction (AVF): $g = \sqrt{1/(1 + MVF/AVF)}$. In practice MVF
comes from a myelin-sensitive measurement such as MTV or magnetization transfer,
and AVF comes from a diffusion model that estimates the intra-axonal water
fraction.

![Geometry of the g-ratio, $g = r/R = \sqrt{1/(1 + MVF/AVF)}$, with the tissue
water compartments and their relaxation times. MVF is the myelin volume fraction;
AVF is the axon volume fraction.](images/ch66/gratio-geometry.png){#fig-ch66-gratio-geometry}

Putting these ingredients together yields whole-brain g-ratio maps from
multi-shell diffusion plus a myelin measurement: separate MVF and AVF maps combine
into a g-ratio map that is relatively uniform across healthy white matter
(@fig-ch66-gratio-whole-brain). The clinical interest is that the g-ratio can
distinguish kinds of tissue damage. In multiple sclerosis, lesions are
hyperintense on FLAIR and reduced on both the MVF and AVF maps, but the g-ratio
map — being a ratio — separates lesions in which myelin and axons are lost
proportionally (g-ratio near normal) from the occasional lesion with
disproportionate myelin loss (elevated g-ratio) (@fig-ch66-gratio-multiple-sclerosis).

![Whole-brain g-ratio from multi-shell DWI. MVF and AVF maps combine into a
g-ratio map that is fairly uniform across healthy white
matter.](images/ch66/gratio-whole-brain.png){#fig-ch66-gratio-whole-brain}

![g-ratio in multiple sclerosis (Stikov et al., 2015). Lesions reduce MVF and AVF,
but most retain a near-normal g-ratio; only one lesion here has a g-ratio above
0.8, indicating disproportionate myelin loss.](images/ch66/gratio-multiple-sclerosis.png){#fig-ch66-gratio-multiple-sclerosis}
